idiom_name: scs SessionManager in the request context with a server-side store (gorilla/sessions FilesystemStore as the smaller alternative)
implementation_notes: Go's standard library HTTP stack is deliberately stateless, so the pattern comes from the ecosystem: scs wires a SessionManager into the middleware chain (sessions.LoadAndSave) and puts the session into the request context, then handlers use session.GetInt/Put/Remove while one of its nineteen server-side stores - Redis, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MSSQL, SQLite and others - holds the record; gorilla/sessions with a FilesystemStore is the older, smaller alternative that still keeps the payload on the server and only a signed id in the cookie. Either way the classic structure (identifier generation, registry, serialization) is provided by the library, and only the store choice and cookie options are left; hand-rolling a map plus sync.RWMutex remains reasonable for a one-process service with a couple of fields.
code_sketch:
sess := scs.New()
sess.Store = redisstore.New(redisClient)          // server-side record
handler := sess.LoadAndSave(app)

http.HandleFunc("/cart", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    n := sess.GetInt(r.Context(), "count")
    sess.Put(r.Context(), "count", n+1)
})
http.ListenAndServe(":8080", handler)
pitfalls: The session is reachable only through the request context, so handlers that take a bare *http.Request from an inner API must pass r.Context() on or they see an empty session.

gorilla/sessions' FilesystemStore still assumes a shared filesystem: behind a load balancer it silently splits conversations unless every instance sees the same disk or the store is swapped for Redis/SQL.
Session values must be serializable with the store's codec (gob or JSON in scs): pointers to live objects, channels or functions cannot cross the store boundary.
